sections.theory:
6.3.8 Confidence interval estimate for the difference between two normal populations means (μ₁ − μ₂) when σ₁², σ₂² are unknown (small sample case)

When population variances are not given and n_1,n_2 are small (< 30) then we have to make another assumption i.e. \sigma_1=\sigma_2=\sigma and this σ is estimated by unbiased pooled estimator. In this case the statistic \overline{X}_1-\overline{X}_2 has the t-distribution with (n_1+n_2-2) degrees of freedom given below;

$t=\frac{(\overline{X}_1-\overline{X}_2)-(\mu_1-\mu_2)}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}}$

where s_p=\sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}}

A 100(1−α)% confidence interval for (\mu_1-\mu_2) in this case is given by

$(\overline{X}_1-\overline{X}_2)\pm t_{\alpha/2,(n_1+n_2-2)}\,s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}$

Example 6.15

The following two samples were randomly selected from two normal populations for which \sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2 but unknown.

Compute 90% confidence interval for the difference between the two population means.

Solution:

100(1−α)% confidence Interval for (\mu_1-\mu_2) in this case is

$(\overline{x}_1-\overline{x}_2)\pm t_{\alpha/2,(n_1+n_2-2)}\,s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}$

Given that

n_1=5,\ \Sigma x_1=492,\ \Sigma x_1^2=48718

n_2=7,\ \Sigma x_2=775,\ \Sigma x_2^2=92019

\text{Now } \overline{x}_1=\frac{\Sigma x_1}{n_1}=\frac{492}{5}=98.4

\overline{x}_2=\frac{\Sigma x_2}{n_2}=\frac{775}{7}=110.71

(n_1-1)s_1^2=\Sigma(x_1-\overline{x}_1)^2=\Sigma x_1^2-\frac{(\Sigma x_1)^2}{n_1}=48718-\frac{(492)^2}{5}=305.2

(n_2-1)s_2^2=\Sigma(x_2-\overline{x}_2)^2=\Sigma x_2^2-\frac{(\Sigma x_2)^2}{n_2}=92019-\frac{(775)^2}{7}=6215.4286

s_p=\sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}}

\text{Now } \overline{x}_1=\frac{\Sigma x_1}{n_1}=\frac{492}{5}=98.4

\overline{x}_2=\frac{\Sigma x_2}{n_2}=\frac{775}{7}=110.71

(n_1-1)s_1^2=\Sigma(x_1-\overline{x}_1)^2=\Sigma x_1^2-\frac{(\Sigma x_1)^2}{n_1}=48718-\frac{(492)^2}{5}=305.2

(n_2-1)s_2^2=\Sigma(x_2-\overline{x}_2)^2=\Sigma x_2^2-\frac{(\Sigma x_2)^2}{n_2}=92019-\frac{(775)^2}{7}=6215.4286

s_p=\sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}}

6.3.8 Confidence interval estimate for the difference between two normal populations means (μ₁ − μ₂) when σ₁², σ₂² are unknown (small sample case)

When population variances are not given and n_1,n_2 are small (< 30) then we have to make another assumption i.e. \sigma_1=\sigma_2=\sigma and this σ is estimated by unbiased pooled estimator. In this case the statistic \overline{X}_1-\overline{X}_2 has the t-distribution with (n_1+n_2-2) degrees of freedom given below;

$t=\frac{(\overline{X}_1-\overline{X}_2)-(\mu_1-\mu_2)}{s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}}$

where s_p=\sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}}

A 100(1−α)% confidence interval for (\mu_1-\mu_2) in this case is given by

$(\overline{X}_1-\overline{X}_2)\pm t_{\alpha/2,(n_1+n_2-2)}\,s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}$

Example 6.15

The following two samples were randomly selected from two normal populations for which \sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2 but unknown.

Compute 90% confidence interval for the difference between the two population means.

Solution:

$(\overline{x}_1-\overline{x}_2)\pm t_{\alpha/2,(n_1+n_2-2)}\,s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}$

n_1=5,\ \Sigma x_1=492,\ \Sigma x_1^2=48718

n_2=7,\ \Sigma x_2=775,\ \Sigma x_2^2=92019
